question: I can't afford to pay my court fines, costs or restitution. Can I get a payment plan, a reduction or waiver, or do community service instead, and what happens if I miss payments?

groups: instead of payment of any fines and court costs

gold_sections.why: The court may order a fine paid at sentencing or in specified installments, payable through a probation agency that must report noncompliance; payment of a fine may be made a condition of probation.

A defendant unable to pay may apply for a reduction; on nonpayment the court may investigate (contumacious vs. indigence) and then commit, reduce the fine, or imprison until payment within capped terms.

Clerk-approved installment plans for traffic fines totaling at least $150 on certification of inability to pay, where the court authorizes the clerk; default leads to Central Collection Unit referral or ordinary processing, with notice.
Unpaid fines and costs are collectable like civil judgments; costs are not part of the penalty and no one may be imprisoned under this subtitle for failing to pay them.

In a criminal case the court may not waive the additional cost imposed under § 7-409 ($45 circuit court, $35 District Court) unless the defendant establishes indigency under the Maryland Rules; it says nothing about waiving other costs.
A court may order community service instead of payment of fines and court costs for a defendant not convicted of a crime of violence.
Community service assignment requires the defendant's consent, is unpaid, and is barred after a crime-of-violence conviction.
Community service programs exist only where a county establishes one (local option).
A court need not order restitution if the obligor lacks the ability to pay or extenuating circumstances make it inappropriate, and must state its reasons.
The restitution subtitle does not limit the court's power to direct the defendant to perform services for the victim as an alternative means of restitution.

Restitution compliance is a condition of probation; payments go to the Department (DPSCS) or Department of Juvenile Services, which may add fees up to 2%; when a payment is overdue the Department notifies the court and requests earnings withholding; the court may hold a contempt or probation-violation hearing, and intentional impoverishment supports a finding against the obligor.

Overdue restitution (30 days default) may be, and after supervision ends must be, referred to the Central Collection Unit, which may certify arrears over $30 for tax refund and lottery interception; compromise needs victim consent.

Earnings withholding orders to collect restitution, which the court may enter when payment is overdue (20% of earnings by default; more if overdue, within federal Consumer Credit Protection Act limits).
A judgment of restitution is a money judgment the victim (or governmental unit or payor) can enforce like a civil judgment.
The $50 monthly probation supervision fee, hardship exemptions, and revocation for nonpayment only after a hearing weighing financial change and good-faith efforts.
Probation violation procedure and caps on incarceration for technical violations.
Probation may be extended to finish making restitution.
Central Collection Unit powers on referred debts: collection fee up to 20%, settlement, fee waiver, tax refund interception, credit reporting.

After an unanswered traffic citation the court may notify the MVA, which must warn of suspension unless within 15 days the person pays, enters a § 7-504.1 payment plan, or requests a new date; it may then suspend, and must withdraw the suspension once the person pays or enters a plan.
If a Vehicle Law fine is not paid and no payment plan is entered, the court may refer it to the Central Collection Unit or process it like other unpaid fines, with notice.
Defines costs and fine (a fine does not include costs).

nuggets.text: After investigating, the court may commit or imprison a defendant who has not paid a fine; imprisonment for default may not exceed 1 day for each $10 of the fine, nor the lesser of one-third of the crime's maximum term or 90 days (15 days for a crime not otherwise jailable), with pro rata credit for time served.

nuggets.quote: Costs are not part of the penalty, and a defendant may not be imprisoned under this subtitle for failure to pay costs.

nuggets.text: If a defendant misses payments under a traffic installment plan, the clerk may refer the unpaid fine to the State's Central Collection Unit (which may add a collection fee of up to 20%, State Finance and Procurement § 3-304) or process it like other unpaid fines, and must notify the defendant; an unpaid Vehicle Law fine with no plan can be referred the same way (Transportation § 27-103).
nuggets.quote: Refer the amount of the unpaid outstanding fine to the Central Collection Unit of the Department of Budget and Management

nuggets.text: If a person does not answer a traffic citation, the court may notify the Motor Vehicle Administration, which must warn that the person's driving privileges will be suspended unless within 15 days of its notice the person pays the fine, enters a § 7-504.1 payment plan, or requests a new trial or hearing date; it may then suspend the license, and must withdraw the suspension once the person pays or enters a plan.

nuggets.text: When a restitution payment is overdue, the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (or Department of Juvenile Services) must notify the court and, if the obligor is employed and no earnings withholding order is in effect, request one; the court may then order the employer to withhold earnings (Criminal Procedure § 11-617).
nuggets.quote: if an earnings withholding order is not in effect and the restitution obligor is employed, request an earnings withholding order

nuggets.text: When restitution is overdue the court may hold a contempt or probation-violation hearing, and if it finds the defendant intentionally became impoverished to avoid paying, it may find contempt or a violation of probation.
nuggets.quote: If the court finds that the restitution obligor intentionally became impoverished to avoid payment of the restitution, the court may find the restitution obligor in contempt of court or in violation of probation.

answer: Yes, mostly at the judge's discretion. A judge may allow fine installments [N1]. For traffic or parking fines of $150 or more, you can certify inability to pay and ask the clerk for a plan [N2]. You may ask the court to reduce a fine you cannot pay [N3]. A court need not order restitution you cannot pay [N7], and the extra § 7-409 conviction cost is waivable only on proof of indigency [N6]. If you consent, your county has a program, and you were not convicted of a crime of violence, the court may order unpaid community service instead of fines and costs [N8]; it may also order services for the victim instead of restitution [N9]. If you miss payments, the court may examine your finances and whether nonpayment is willful or due to poverty [N4], then cut the fine to what you can pay [N5] or jail you, up to 1 day per $10 within other caps [N10]; federal law generally bars jailing people who truly cannot pay. You cannot be jailed for unpaid costs, but fines and costs can be collected like civil judgments [N11]. Missed traffic plan payments can go to the State's Central Collection Unit [N12]; an unanswered traffic ticket can get your license suspended unless you pay, enter a plan or request a new date within 15 days of the MVA's notice [N13]. Overdue restitution can bring wage withholding [N14] and a contempt or probation-violation hearing; deliberately impoverishing yourself counts against you [N15].

gaps: Courts Article § 7-504(c) lets the court, after investigating, commit the defendant, reduce the fine, or imprison until payment, without stating when each applies, so nonpayment_ruling models the choice as court discretion. The investigation looks at whether nonpayment is contumacious or due to indigence (§ 7-504(b)); the rule that a court may not jail someone who cannot pay despite bona fide efforts comes from federal constitutional law (Bearden v. Georgia, 461 U.S. 660 (1983)), not the Maryland text.

Court costs: a criminal court may not waive the additional § 7-409 cost ($45 in circuit court, $35 in District Court for a crime; $3 for a non-jailable traffic offense) unless the defendant establishes indigency under the Maryland Rules (Courts § 7-405); no statute found governs waiving other costs. No one may be imprisoned under the subtitle for failure to pay costs (§ 7-505(b)); unpaid fines and costs may instead be collected like civil judgments (§ 7-505(a)). These are not modeled as steps.

The clerk installment plan (Courts § 7-504.1) covers only fines for traffic offenses, including parking citations, totaling at least $150, and only where the District Court or a circuit court has authorized the clerk; agreeing to pay a payable citation by installments consents to conviction. An unpaid Vehicle Law fine with no plan may likewise be referred to the Central Collection Unit (Transportation § 27-103). What 'process the unpaid outstanding fine as it would other outstanding fines' involves is not stated. License suspension for an unanswered traffic citation (Transportation § 26-204) is not modeled as steps.

Community service instead of fines and costs (Correctional Services § 8-703) requires the defendant's consent, is unpaid, is unavailable after a conviction for a crime of violence (§ 8-704), and depends on a county community service program (§ 8-702). Services for the victim instead of restitution (Criminal Procedure § 11-619(b)) are at the court's discretion and are not modeled.

Restitution: a court need not order it if the defendant cannot pay (Criminal Procedure § 11-605); that question is raised when restitution is ordered, and no section found in the downloaded code lets the court reduce restitution afterward, while the Central Collection Unit may compromise it only with the victim's consent (§ 11-616(c)). Restitution is overdue if unpaid by the court's date or, if none, by the later of the Division's date or 30 days after judgment (§ 11-616(e)); overdue accounts may (and once supervision ends must) go to the Central Collection Unit (§ 11-616(a)), the victim may enforce the judgment like a civil money judgment (§ 11-608), and probation may be extended to finish restitution (§ 6-222(b)).

pay_fine covers fine installments the court orders paid to a probation agency (Courts § 7-503(b)); fines paid to the court directly are not modeled. pay_restitution follows the restitution payment duty to the Department (Criminal Procedure § 11-607(b)). The court may enter an earnings withholding order when restitution is overdue without a hearing (§ 11-617(a)(2)(iii)).

Payment of a fine may be made a condition of probation (Courts § 7-503(c)) and compliance with restitution must be (Criminal Procedure § 11-607(a)(1)(iii)), so a missed payment can be charged as a probation violation. Probation supervision fees ($50 a month, Criminal Procedure § 6-226) and revocation for nonpayment (§ 6-226(f), § 6-223) are not modeled as steps; a missed payment that involves no new arrest, crime, no-contact violation or absconding fits the definition of a technical violation (Correctional Services § 6-101(m), not a gold section), for which § 6-223(d) presumptively caps incarceration at 15, 30 and 45 days for the first three.

local_option: Community service instead of fines and costs depends on a county community service program: a county may establish one (Correctional Services § 8-702), run by the county or by the Division of Parole and Probation within the county (§ 8-706). The clerk installment plan for traffic fines is available where the District Court or a circuit court authorizes the clerk (Courts § 7-504.1(b)).
notes: Maryland statutes only, as downloaded. No effective-date variants were found for the gold sections. Courts § 7-504.1 is limited to traffic offenses (including parking); other fines rely on the court's installment power in § 7-503 and the reduction remedy in § 7-504. Nuggets are capped at 15, so some correct points live in the gold sections, steps, gaps and nugget texts without a nugget of their own: the $50 monthly supervision fee and its hardship exemptions (Criminal Procedure § 6-226), the Central Collection Unit's collection fee of up to 20% and its power to report accounts to consumer reporting agencies (State Finance and Procurement § 3-304), referral of overdue restitution to the Central Collection Unit and tax refund and lottery interception for arrears over $30 (Criminal Procedure § 11-616), and enforcement of restitution as a civil money judgment (§ 11-608), which in circuit court is also recorded as a lien on land (§ 11-609, not a gold section). Earnings withholding for restitution defaults to 20% of earnings, but the court may order more when restitution is overdue, within the federal Consumer Credit Protection Act limits (§ 11-617(e)); the Department may also charge fees of up to 2% of the restitution judgment for collection (§ 11-607(b)(2)(iii)). Traffic citations must warn that failing to act within 30 days may lead to license suspension (Transportation § 26-201(c), not a gold section). Municipal infractions (Local Government § 6-110: the court may suspend or defer the fine) and county civil infractions (Local Government § 11-209: willful failure to pay may be treated as criminal contempt) are outside this answer.
